newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PacDun sees much stronger 2nd half.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PacDun sees much stronger 2nd half.

text.p: Pacific Dunlop Ltd said on Friday it expected to report a much stronger performance in the second half of the financial year ending June 30, due in part to an improvement in its battery division.
"We are confident that the second six month period will be much stronger than the first six months," Pacific Dunlop Managing Director Rod Chadwick told reporters.
Pacific Dunlop, an industrial conglomerate exposed to the consumer, building and automotive sectors, reported a net profit before abnormals of A$118 million for the first half of 1995/96.
Chadwick said improvements at the battery division's troubled Colombus lead smelter in the United States would underpin a profit recovery in the current half.
The 90,000-tonnes-a-year smelter would be ramped up to near-fill capacity by around June, Chadwick said.
"Obviously, I am expecting a better result out of GNB (battery division)," he said.
The other five of Pacific Dunlop's six operating groups are all performing broadly in line with expectations, Chadwick said.
He forecast Pacific Brands, the group's clothing and footwear division, to post a much stronger second half compared with the second half of 1995/96.

He also saw "upside" in the cables division and said the group's drive to find effiencies in its Australian manufacturing base, and move to third-party manufacturing offshore, would also help lift the bottom line for the full year.
"All of these things I think will add to a stronger result," Chadwick said.
Pacific Dunlop reported a 28 percent drop in net profit to A$84 million in the first half-year ended December 31.
The battery division's earnings dived 98 percent from a year ago to just A$1 million. Its result included a A$12.3 million charge for write-offs of obsolete equipment and facilities.
Pacific Dunlop has forecast its annual earnings for 1996/97 to still be higher than 1995/96, when the group reported a pre-abnormal net profit of A$162 million.
The group closed eight manufacturing sites, shed around 2,000 jobs and sold five non-core operations in the first half-year, Chadwick said.
He said the group's assets were now more tightly managed and that Pacific Dunlop was poised to "take off" once the domestic economy picked up.
Pacific Dunlop shares closed three cents firmer at A$3.16 on Friday.
